item.title: The simulability frontiers of photonic quantum computing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a concrete benchmark—one exact sample per second on a fixed classical machine—that lets researchers compare photonic devices across architectures and algorithms on equal footing, something the field has lacked amid wildly varying photon‑count thresholds. By releasing an open‑source GPU library and reporting that state‑of‑the‑art H100 hardware can still be classically simulated up to roughly 38 single photons (or 31 entangled photons), it quantifies how far current photonic platforms are from the “quantum advantage” regime while highlighting that algorithmic gains shift the frontier more than raw speed. The work therefore provides a practical yardstick for future hardware upgrades and for assessing claims of quantum supremacy in boson‑sampling–type experiments.

Estimates of when photonic devices outgrow classical simulation are hard to compare: even for single-photon boson sampling, quoted thresholds range from 50 to 98 photons, as they rest on different tasks and assumptions. We propose as a common unit the time a classical computer needs to draw one sample from the device's exact output distribution, up to floating-point rounding. Only exactness applies equally to every kind of light, since the cost of approximate sampling depends on the accuracy required. The simulability frontier is the device size at which our fastest exact sampler produces one sample per second on a fixed machine; this device size increases with better hardware and algorithms. As the time per sample grows exponentially with the number of detected photons, doubling the machine speed moves the frontier by about one photon, whereas a better algorithm changes the growth rate. We measure the frontier with photonic-engines, an open-source GPU library of exact samplers for single photons, entangled photons from quantum emitters, vacuum-single-photon superpositions and squeezed light. Each sampler is validated against a simulator sharing no code with it. On one NVIDIA H100 GPU, with Haar-random interferometers, twice as many modes as photonic inputs and photon-number-resolving detectors, the frontier lies at 38.3 single photons and at 31.0 entangled photons from one emitter. For squeezed light, a timing model fitted to measurements places it at 41.5 squeezed photonic inputs of mean photon number 0.5. For our samplers, coherence alone makes simulation harder: sources that emit a photon with probability one half reach 64.2 when vacuum and photon are mixed incoherently, as for lossy single photons, but only 50.0 when they are in coherent superposition. Feed-forward from mid-circuit measurement of up to three modes lowers the single-photon frontier only from 38.3 to 38.1.

item.title: Physics Reports Analysis Evaluates Emergence of Hybrid Semiconductor–Superconducting Qubit Architectures
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article spotlights the growing momentum behind hybrid semiconductor‑superconductor qubits, whose electrostatic tunability and intrinsic noise protection could fill niche functions that pure transmons struggle with—such as flux‑free couplers or spin‑to‑microwave interfaces. By situating these devices alongside recent advances in gate‑tunable transmons and Majorana research, the review underscores a broader industry shift toward heterogeneous quantum processors rather than a wholesale replacement of existing hardware. Readers should note that while the architectures promise higher coherence and specialized memory capabilities, their practical deployment will still hinge on scaling challenges and integration with established superconducting stacks.

A new review in Physics Reports examines hybrid semiconductor-superconductor qubits, highlighting their development and various architectures like gate-tunable transmons and fluxoniums, Andreev level qubits, and Majorana-based parity qubits. These qubits offer unique advantages such as electrostatic frequency control, enhanced coherence, and noise protection. While not expected to replace current commercial qubits for general computing, their specialized roles in heterogeneous processors could include flux-free tunable couplers, spin-to-microwave interconnects, and non-local topological memories. item.title: DLR Develops Scalable Unitary Data Encoding Beating Exponential State-Preparation Depth
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article highlights a breakthrough in quantum data loading by showing that classical vectors can be encoded with sub‑linear circuit depth instead of the traditionally exponential cost, a bottleneck that has limited many near‑term algorithms. By marrying tensor‑network compression with Boolean logic minimization and Walsh–Hadamard transforms, the DLR team demonstrates a scalable approach that already runs on a 20‑qubit processor, positioning it as a practical tool for quantum machine learning, finance and chemistry where large data sets must be fed into quantum circuits. The result narrows the gap between theoretical speedups and hardware realities, though its performance will still depend on error rates and connectivity in larger devices. Readers should watch how this encoding scheme integrates with upcoming variational algorithms, as it could markedly improve overall runtime and fidelity.

Researchers at the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and the University of Cologne developed a new quantum state-preparation framework that significantly reduces circuit depth for loading classical data onto quantum computers. Their method, combining tensor networks, Boolean logic minimization, and Walsh-Hadamard transformations, achieves sub-linear depth scaling and was validated on a 20-qubit quantum processor. This advancement addresses a critical bottleneck in quantum algorithms, enabling more efficient state initialization for various applications. item.title: Unified architecture for arbitrary two-qubit gates with neutral atoms
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that neutral‑atom processors can natively generate any two‑qubit gate by exploiting a single tunable XXZ interaction together with standard single‑qubit rotations, eliminating the need to decompose algorithms into a limited native set such as CZ or CNOT. By showing concrete Rydberg implementations of gates ranging from B and QFT to iSWAP and a continuous family interpolating between CZ and iSWAP, the work bridges a gap that has long constrained compilation efficiency on atom‑based hardware. The ability to switch instruction sets on the fly promises shallower circuits and reduced overhead for near‑term algorithms, though experimental realization will still hinge on precise control of anisotropy and microwave driving fidelity.

We propose a unified architecture for two-qubit gates in neutral-atom quantum processors which allows the implementation of the complete set of two-qubit gates. Our approach rests on a single resource that unlocks the entire gate set: an XXZ interaction with tunable anisotropy, combined only with single-qubit operations. We introduce a Rydberg-atom realization of the tunable XXZ interaction and combine it with optimally controlled global microwave pulses to implement the B, QFT, iSWAP, and $\sqrt{\mathrm{iSWAP}}$ gates, as well as a continuous gate family interpolating from CZ to iSWAP via the B gate. This work allows the implementation of any two-qubit gate natively in neutral-atom platforms, enabling flexible switching between instruction sets to reduce circuit depth and compilation overhead in quantum algorithm implementation.

item.title: IonQ and Classiq Outline Architectural Trade-Offs in Fault-Tolerant Resource Estimation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it overturns the long‑standing assumption that cutting non‑Clifford gate counts alone drives fault‑tolerant performance, showing instead that magic‑state preparation efficiencies have shifted the bottleneck to routing overhead, Clifford operations and qubit idle times. By quantifying how these factors dominate the physical spacetime volume, IonQ and Classiq make a strong case for full‑stack compilation tools that co‑optimize logical circuits, error‑correction codes and hardware layout—a direction echoed by recent efforts at Google and IBM to integrate surface‑code aware schedulers. Readers should take away that future resource estimates will need to account for architecture‑level trade‑offs, not just algorithmic gate counts, before realistic quantum advantage timelines can be set.

IonQ and Classiq's analysis shows that minimizing non-Clifford gates is no longer the primary factor in fault-tolerant quantum computing performance. Advances in magic state preparation mean that routing, Clifford gates, and memory retention now significantly impact the overall physical spacetime volume. Therefore, a full-stack compilation approach considering physical layouts and error correction is crucial for accurate evaluation of fault-tolerant algorithms. item.title: Sequential vs parallel Strategies for Sharing Quantum Advantage in Communication Tasks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints a sharp boundary between sequential and parallel ways of distributing quantum advantage, showing that while two observers can always mimic a parallel protocol with a sequential one, adding a third observer creates statistics that only true parallel sharing can achieve. By proving the impossibility of parallel sharing for standard 3‑bit random access codes yet demonstrating it for parity‑oblivious RACs, the work clarifies which communication tasks are fundamentally limited by measurement disturbance—a key insight for designing multi‑user quantum networks and distributed sensing platforms. The results dovetail with recent advances in quantum repeaters and clone‑based protocols, suggesting that careful task selection will be essential to harness sustainable quantum resources across many parties.

Information can be extracted from a quantum system in a sustainable manner, allowing the system to be reused for further information extraction through subsequent interactions. We investigate the possibility of consensus between two experimentally feasible methods, namely, parallel and sequential sharing, that enable multiple observers to extract information encoded in a quantum system. We show that any statistics generated by a parallel sharing strategy can be reproduced by a sequential strategy when only two observers are involved. However, when more than two observers participate in sharing quantum correlations, certain statistics achievable through parallel strategies cannot be reproduced by sequential strategies. Moreover, we demonstrate that sharing quantum advantage through a parallel strategy is impossible for a class of communication tasks involving two decoding measurements, thereby establishing an arbitrarily large gap between the sustainability of quantum advantage under sequential and parallel strategies. This naturally raises the question of whether this impossibility extends to communication tasks involving more than two decoding measurements. We show that, while parallel sharing of quantum advantage is impossible in a 3-bit random access code (RAC), it becomes possible in a 3-bit parity-oblivious RAC, where at most two observers can simultaneously obtain a quantum advantage by performing measurements on two imperfect clones of the initially prepared quantum system. Our findings have potential applications in the development of quantum communication networks and distributed quantum information processing.

item.title: Quantum Residual Exploration for Selected Configuration Interaction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a hybrid quantum‑classical workflow that lets a trapped‑ion processor suggest new determinants for selected configuration interaction, accepting only those that improve the variational energy relative to purely classical candidates. By targeting multistep excitations that perturbative schemes often miss, it demonstrates a measurable energy gain for a stretched H₁₂ chain while keeping the total determinant count fixed—a clear step toward more efficient quantum‑assisted electronic‑structure methods. The result shows how modest near‑term devices can augment traditional algorithms, though scaling to larger molecules will still require advances in error mitigation and hardware connectivity.

We propose a modular hybrid quantum-classical method to improve selected configuration interaction at a fixed final determinant budget. Quantum measurements supply complementary determinants, accepted only when they outrank classical candidates under a common energetic criterion. This targets multistep excitations that perturbative discovery may miss in strongly correlated systems. A demonstration on the Quantinuum Reimei trapped-ion quantum computer shows that measured proposals for H$_{12}$ at a stretched geometry lower the variational energy relative to classical-only selection at the same final determinant budget.

item.title: All-to-all connectivity via adiabatic ZZ interactions in a superconducting flux qubit processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a way to achieve true all‑to‑all connectivity in a superconducting flux‑qubit processor by using baseband‑driven adiabatic ZZ interactions mediated through a common cavity, allowing any pair of qubits to be entangled while the devices remain at their flux sweet spots. By tilting the quantization axes with low‑frequency drives rather than relying on resonant couplers, the scheme sidesteps the bulky wiring and control overhead that currently limit scalability, and numerical simulations predict coherent errors below 10⁻⁴ even when multiple gates run in parallel. If experimentally realized, this approach could dramatically simplify hardware layouts for large‑scale quantum simulators and error‑corrected processors, though practical implementation will need to confirm robustness against real‑world noise and fabrication variations.

Scalable superconducting quantum processors would benefit from high qubit connectivity, yet existing architectures connect neighbouring qubits via tunable couplers, which introduce substantial wiring and control overhead. Here, we propose a baseband-driven adiabatic ZZ gate that entangles any selected pair in a register of flux qubits coupled via a common cavity. The qubits stay dc-biased at their flux sweet spot. Strong drives applied selectively through local flux lines, at frequencies far below the qubit transitions, adiabatically tilt the quantization axes and generate an effective longitudinal ZZ interaction. The strength of the coupling is tunable and controlled by the amplitudes and relative phase of the drives rather than by any resonance condition. Numerical simulations give coherent gate errors below $10^{-4}$ over broad ranges of drive frequency, with comparable fidelities for two simultaneous gates in a four-qubit register. The protocol is robust against frequency fluctuations and remains effective even when many qubits are coupled to the cavity.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: An Alternative to Quantum Theory
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article proposes a radical, scale‑invariant ontology that seeks to reproduce all quantum predictions without invoking wavefunctions or dynamical evolution, offering a fresh angle on the long‑standing measurement and entanglement puzzles. By grounding observable phenomena in simple ratios of masses, charges and separations among point particles, it connects to earlier “hidden‑variable” approaches while sidestepping many of their technical hurdles, potentially reshaping how we think about atomistic structure and macroscopic emergence. If the framework can be extended to concrete sensing protocols or experimental tests, it could open a new pathway toward theory‑driven device design, but at present its claims remain highly speculative and will require rigorous validation against established quantum results.

Despite the remarkable empirical success of quantum theory, the interpretation of measurement and the nature of entanglement correlations remain open questions. We outline an alternative framework that seeks to recover the empirical results of quantum theory from a holistic, scale-invariant ontology. Assuming only point particles in Euclidean space, characterised by ratios of masses (and charges) and by the ratios of their mutual separations, the theory describes shapes through a single scale-invariant function; no dynamical evolution is required. In principle, this framework provides a unified description of finite subsystems embedded in a configuration of infinitely many particles and offers a possible route to deriving the observed structures of atoms, molecules and macroscopic bodies without invoking standard quantum mechanics.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Universal two-qubit control across dilution refrigerators via a 10-km coherent optical link
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first coherent optical link that can ferry microwave control pulses and phase references across a 10‑km fiber to operate superconducting qubits in separate dilution refrigerators, effectively providing a classical “backbone” for modular quantum processors. By achieving universal two‑qubit gates and an 80 % Bell‑state fidelity between a transmon and a cavity qubit located in different cryostats, the work bridges a gap between on‑chip control and long‑distance quantum networking that earlier experiments could only address within a single fridge. The result opens a realistic path toward scalable distributed architectures for computation, communication and sensing, although further improvements in transducer efficiency will be needed to push fidelities into fault‑tolerant regimes.

Distributed quantum networks are important for scalable quantum processors and for potential applications in communication, distributed computation, and sensing, in which direct classical links for adaptive control are essential to harness the shared entanglement. However, controlling superconducting quantum processors from a separate refrigerator over long distances remains elusive. Here, we introduce a coherent optical link (COL) that delivers microwave waveforms and their phase references between dilution refrigerators. Combining a laser, a microwave-to-optical transducer and an optical-to-microwave photodiode, the COL transmits microwave control signals over 10~km of fiber, while optical references derived from the same laser compensate for the frequency mismatch between devices. Through the COL, we deliver a universal gate set to a transmon qubit and a cavity qubit in another refrigerator and entangle them, and achieve a Bell-state fidelity of 80.6\%. Quantum control delivered through the COL thus provides a classical backbone for modular quantum processors.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Deploying QKD on the fiber links of the National Quantum Communication Infrastructure in Sweden
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that Sweden’s national fiber network can support continuous‑time quantum key distribution, providing the first long‑duration field validation of QKD performance on real‑world telecom links in Europe. By systematically mapping loss, dispersion and noise against a simplified secret‑key‑rate model, the authors create a practical toolkit for operators to assess any existing backbone before retrofitting it with quantum security hardware. The month‑long successful run demonstrates that large‑scale rollout of QKD is no longer a laboratory curiosity but an imminent service, although scaling to higher rates will still depend on improving detector efficiency and managing fiber aging.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) is being deployed across Europe to evaluate its performance and practicality in real-world scenarios. When preparing this deployment, it is important to survey the properties of the fiber links that will be used for the quantum channel, cross-checking them with those of QKD devices, to ensure compatibility and optimal performance. We report here our studies from the Swedish chapter of this endeavor, the National Quantum Communication Infrastructure in Sweden. We focus on procedures to characterize the links and evaluate their suitability for QKD. We relate measurable properties to the key factors that affect the secret key rate using a simplified model that aims at the essence of QKD performance. Finally, we confirm the feasibility of QKD on one of our links by reporting a one-month long successful test.

item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Commuting-check gauging for fault-tolerant logical measurements
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces “completion” qubits that turn non‑commuting gauge checks into a commuting set while preserving the code distance and low‑density parity‑check structure, offering a constant‑factor overhead solution to a long‑standing obstacle in fault‑tolerant logical measurement. By guaranteeing global commutation, the authors achieve a logical measurement whose circuit fault distance scales linearly with the parent code distance using only O(d) measurement rounds—a clear improvement over earlier lattice‑surgery schemes that required more complex ancilla handling or higher overhead. The result opens a practical pathway for scalable magic‑state preparation and other fault‑tolerant operations, though its current demonstration is limited to toric‑code examples and prime‑dimensional qudits, so broader code families will need further validation.

Gauging turns a logical operator into a product of local checks, providing a route to logical measurement and lattice surgery. These checks can fail to commute outside the code space, so measuring one can randomize the outcome of another. In this work, we introduce completion qubits that make the checks commute for Clifford $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetries of qubit stabilizer codes. Adding one completion qubit per noncommuting pair preserves the gauged code space and its distance while keeping the checks Clifford. Completion also preserves the low-density parity-check property with a constant-factor qubit overhead. We generalize completion to qudits and establish bounds on the Clifford-hierarchy level of the completed checks in prime dimensions. Global commutation ensures that a fault-free round fixes the syndrome until the next fault and allows us to bound fault propagation independently of the number of measurement rounds. For qubit codes, we show that gauging and ungauging a distance-$d$ parent code implements a logical measurement with circuit fault distance $Ω(d)$ in $O(d)$ rounds. We demonstrate the construction by gauging two toric codes into the $D(D_4)$ quantum double and back, with an explicit circuit whose circuit fault distance equals the parent code distance. Our results provide a framework for fault-tolerant logical measurements using commuting checks, with applications to magic-state preparation by lattice surgery.

item.title: Testing non-classical gravitational phase dynamics under strong dephasing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a genuine quantum‑gravity signature can survive even when decoherence suppresses entanglement, by exploiting the conditional phase accumulated in a dephased Bose–Marletto–Vedral interferometer. It extends recent BMV‑type proposals into the experimentally realistic strong‑dephasing regime, offering an operational test that distinguishes a quantum Newtonian potential from any passive stochastic classical mediator. While the result hinges on specific assumptions about local‑phase noise models, it gives experimentalists a concrete pathway to probe gravitational coherence with current matter‑wave technology.

Whether gravity must be quantum is often approached by asking whether two masses can become entangled through their mutual gravitational interaction. In practice, the weak interaction competes with environmental decoherence, so the final state may contain no entanglement even when the underlying gravitational phase remains coherent. We investigate what can still be learned from the dynamics in a dephased Bose--Marletto--Vedral setup. The dominant Newtonian effect for well-separated paths is an accumulated phase rather than transfer between interferometer arms, a regime motivated by matter-wave gravitational phase experiments and quantified here by wavepacket-overlap and deflection estimates. Keeping independently characterized local which-path dephasing fixed, we prove an exact finite-time distinction between the gravitational conditional-phase evolution and every passive stochastic local-phase model (induced by a classical mediator), including regimes where the chosen input remains separable at all times. The distinction survives, with a modified sensitivity, when the comparison is enlarged to population-preserving classical measurement and feedback through a diagonal PPT relaxation. These results identify an operational test of gravitational phase dynamics in the strong-dephasing regimes, conditional on explicit and physically motivated classical mediator models.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Modular and Looping Quantum Photonic Processing Unit for Quantum Computing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a truly modular, loop‑based photonic architecture that promises universal, deterministic quantum computation while dramatically cutting the number of required optical components—a long‑standing bottleneck for scaling photonic processors. By proving compatibility with the standard circuit model and demonstrating reprogrammability through adaptive measurements, the work builds on recent time‑bin and integrated‑photonics advances and shows how machine‑learning‑optimized linear and nonlinear elements can be assembled into a practical hardware blueprint. If realized experimentally, the design could accelerate the transition from proof‑of‑concept boson‑sampling devices to fully programmable quantum processors with far lower fabrication overhead.

Photonic processors are emerging as promising platforms in the race towards the realization of practical universal quantum computers. Several architectures with universal capabilities have been proposed for their implementation via a photonic platform, each with their own set of benefits and drawbacks. In this work we propose an architecture for a universal photonic quantum computer. The proposed architecture is modular, allowing for a high degree of flexibility and scalability, and relies on a loop-based structure, significantly reducing the number of physical components required to implement it experimentally. We prove that our architecture is universal, deterministic, and compatible with the quantum circuital model, as well as reprogrammable and capable of adaptive measurements. Furthermore, we showcase its functioning via numerical simulation on specific examples, by using machine learning techniques on a set of fundamental linear and nonlinear optical components to obtain some of the building blocks used in the architecture. The obtained results can be used to highlight the benefits and the drawbacks of the proposed architecture, as well as the route for future developments towards its physical implementation.

item.title: A Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Architecture with Globally Driven Atom Arrays
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that a globally driven, dual‑species neutral‑atom platform can reach fault‑tolerant thresholds above 1 % without the need for individually addressed laser beams, a long‑standing bottleneck for scaling up atom‑based processors. By leveraging interspecies Rydberg interactions to achieve selective control and compiling surface‑code cycles into the new GRAIL instruction set, the authors push logical error rates toward the 10⁻⁹ regime—comparable to recent breakthroughs in superconducting and trapped‑ion systems but with far simpler hardware overhead. If experimental Rydberg Rabi frequencies can meet the modest requirements outlined, this architecture could accelerate the transition from small testbeds to truly large‑scale quantum computers built on neutral atoms.

Scalable quantum computation requires reconciling programmability with simple, high-fidelity control. Here, we propose a universal fault-tolerant architecture using globally driven dual-species atom arrays. In a hybrid neutral-atom system, interspecies Rydberg interactions enable qubit addressability without locally addressed quantum gates. We construct a universal native instruction set, Global Rydberg Atom Instruction Language (GRAIL), and show that crosstalk errors can be suppressed to the $10^{-4}$ level. We compile surface-code error correction and magic state cultivation into GRAIL, and parallelize the compilation to suppress crosstalk. Under a hardware-inferred circuit-level noise model, we obtain an error-correction threshold of $1.43\%$ for the resulting quantum memory and a logical error rate below $10^{-9}$ for magic states cultivated at an experimentally accessible Rydberg Rabi frequency. By replacing local gate addressing with atom-mediated selectivity, this architecture removes the associated calibration requirements, offering a route to simpler control for large-scale fault-tolerant neutral-atom computation.

item.title: Rapid high-purity loading of barium ion via relayed selectivity from naturally abundant source
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a UV‑free three‑step photoionization protocol that can load a single barium isotope with >99 % purity directly from a natural source, eliminating the need for costly isotopically enriched ovens and reducing background contamination. By exploiting narrow‑band resonances at 791 nm and 554 nm before ionizing with an existing 532 nm Raman beam, the authors achieve both rapid loading rates and “relayed selectivity,” a technique that could be adapted to other trapped‑ion species as labs push toward larger, mixed‑isotope quantum processors. The result speeds up qubit initialization and simplifies hardware, addressing a bottleneck that has limited scaling in ion‑trap architectures despite recent advances in high‑fidelity gates and modular trap designs.

Trapped ions is one of the promising platforms for realizing quantum information processing and quantum simulation. Selective and rapid loading of a specific isotope lays the critical foundation for such purpose particularly when scaling up the system size. Here we demonstrate a new method for rapid isotope-selective loading of $^{137}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$ or $^{135}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$, two types of promising ion qubits, from naturally abundant source using a three-step, ultraviolet-free photoionization scheme. Neutral atoms are selected on the narrow 791 nm $6s^2\,{}^1S_0\rightarrow6s6p\,{}^3P_1^o$ transition, resonantly transferred at 554 nm to $6s6d\,{}^3D_1$, and ionized using an existing 532 nm Raman beam. A spectral-overlap analysis based on isotope and hyperfine shifts shows relayed selectivity that the second step can further suppress undesired-isotope excitation and no contaminant ion is detected during our entire experiment. Besides, the resonant drive of the second step excitation yields a prominent loading rate of the selected species. This strategy using multi-step excitations to establish relayed selectivity can be extended to high-purity loading of other species of ions.

item.title: Long-distance quantum secure direct communication with Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows for the first time how Gottesman‑Kitaev‑Preskill (GKP) error correction can be harnessed to build a quantum‑secure direct‑communication link that survives more than 1 000 km of fiber, thanks to third‑generation repeater techniques and only modest 23 dB squeezing. By coupling the lattice‑based GKP code with an optimization framework for repeater placement, the work bridges the gap between theoretical error‑corrected channels and practical network design, offering a concrete pathway toward large‑scale quantum‑secure messaging. The results push QSDC from laboratory demos toward real‑world cryptographic infrastructure, although achieving the required squeezing and low‑loss repeaters remains an experimental challenge.

The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code possesses a lattice periodic structure that enables the effective correction of small displacement errors induced by noise in phase space, which is indispensable for quantum computation. The GKP code was also used to construct a long-distance entanglement channel in quantum repeaters and distribute random keys in quantum key distribution (QKD). Using GKP encoding, we propose a quantum secure direct communication (QSDC) protocol that not only transmits the secret message directly, but also helps protect the safety of communication personnel. The exponential attenuation loss of photons can be overcome by the third-generation quantum repeater. Numerical simulation results demonstrate that secure transmission distance exceeding 1000 km is achievable with a 23 dB squeezing level. Furthermore, we establish a cost-based optimization framework to characterize the trade-off among secure communication distance, secrecy capacity, and repeater resources, enabling optimized repeater deployment and providing a systematic design strategy for scalable quantum repeater architectures. The results demonstrate the potential of combining GKP error correction for long-distance QSDC and quantum networks.

item.title: Trajectory-Dependent Decoherence and Leakage During Shuttling of Multi-Spin Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a key bottleneck for scalable semiconductor quantum computers by quantifying how the path taken during electron‑spin shuttling directly shapes decoherence and leakage in multi‑spin logical qubits. By deriving compact fidelity formulas that depend only on experimentally accessible pairwise dephasing rates, the authors give hardware teams concrete criteria for choosing parallel versus sequential transport regimes—a distinction that aligns with recent demonstrations of long‑range spin conveyance and emerging fault‑tolerant architectures. The work therefore bridges theory and practice, offering a roadmap to minimize noise‑induced errors as qubit shuttling becomes a central element of future quantum processors.

Logical qubits encoded in collective states of multiple spins are promising building blocks for large-scale semiconductor quantum processors. As novel fault-tolerant architectures increasingly rely on qubit shuttling, understanding decoherence of the shuttled multi-spin qubits becomes crucial. We analyze fidelity and leakage of the logical qubits dephased by the spatio-temporally correlated $1/f$ noise, considering two-, three-, and four-spin encodings. We study different shuttling protocols and establish that for all encodings generally, parallel shuttling provides the best protection against decoherence at short distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms others for long-range transport (although the exact boundaries depend on the specific device parameters). We explain this common behavior in terms of the dephasing factors of pairs of the shuttled spins; we provide explicit expressions for fidelities and leakage, thus enabling experimentalists to predict performance of the multi-spin qubits from only several independently measured pairwise dephasing factors. Our results establish a connection between shuttling trajectories, noise correlations, and qubit decoherence, and provide guidance for achieving noise-resilient shuttling in scalable semiconductor quantum processors.

item.title: Arrival-time problem in the quantum information era - observation of a Zeno crossover in monitored arrival-time distributions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles the classic “when does a quantum particle arrive?” question by demonstrating that monitored transport on superconducting processors exhibits a clear crossover between a quantum‑Zeno regime and a low‑monitoring regime, with an optimal measurement cadence set by the particle’s bandwidth. By confirming the theory across single‑particle, interacting many‑body, and two‑dimensional circuits, the work shows that Zeno‑type control is a generic tool for shaping dynamical information flow in quantum hardware—a capability that could be leveraged for error mitigation, state preparation, or quantum sensing protocols. The results also provide the first experimental arrival‑time distributions in a monitored setting, establishing a new benchmark for quantum‑trajectory modeling on near‑term devices.

When does a quantum particle arrive at a detector? The temporal distributions of itinerant quantum particles have been debated since the birth of quantum mechanics. Here we study the arrival-time problem in periodically monitored spin chains and quantum circuits. The arrival dynamics exhibits two regimes, the quantum Zeno and the low-monitoring regime, separated by an optimal monitoring period set by the single-particle bandwidth. In support of the theory, on superconducting quantum hardware, we measure arrival-time distributions for single and multiple interacting particles in one- and two-dimensional circuits. The measured distributions resolve both regimes and agree closely with quantum-trajectory theory. The crossover persists in interacting many-particle systems: the optimal monitoring point is preserved while many-body interference reshapes the distributions. Zeno suppression likewise persists in two-dimensional geometry. Together, these results show that the two regimes are a generic feature of monitored propagation rather than a single-particle effect. To our knowledge, our work constitutes the first experimental measurement of arrival-time distributions in a monitored quantum transport setting, addressing one of the longest-standing problems in quantum mechanics.

item.title: Scalable Unitary State-Encoding for Generic Large Data
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles the long‑standing data‑loading bottleneck by presenting deterministic, low‑depth amplitude‑encoding circuits that scale to arbitrarily large vectors without requiring amplitude amplification or mid‑circuit measurement. By recasting multi‑controlled rotations as a Boolean minimisation problem and exploiting an ancilla‑based Walsh–Hadamard decomposition, the authors achieve order‑of‑magnitude reductions in two‑qubit gate count compared with Qiskit’s default state‑preparation routine—a gain they validate on IQM’s square‑lattice hardware. The result opens a practical pathway for near‑term quantum‑machine‑learning and variational algorithms that depend on fast, high‑fidelity state preparation, though the reported depth advantages assume relatively flexible connectivity and may diminish on more constrained devices.

Efficient encoding of data into quantum states remains a fundamental bottleneck in many quantum computing protocols, which would otherwise offer advantages over their classical counterparts. Here, we introduce deterministic and scalable amplitude-encoding methods with low two-qubit gate costs and tunable trade-offs between circuit depth and encoding fidelity. Our approaches require no amplitude amplification or mid-circuit measurement and are capable of encoding arbitrary complex data or queryable functions by using tensor-networks to go beyond what can be held in classical memory. Our principle contributions are two complementary algorithms for simplifying fully controlled multiplexer circuits to one- and two-qubit gates. In the first, we formally map the elimination of redundant gate controls to a Boolean logic minimization problem, while in the second we utilize a single ancilla qubit to map the multi-controlled rotation gates to a sequence of one- and two-qubit operations via the Walsh-Hadamard spectrum of the gate angles. We benchmark these methods across a broad range of function classes, characterizing their total depth in an all-to-all connectivity graph against system size and target fidelity. Hybridizing our methods gives up to orders of magnitude improvement in circuit depth at equivalent state fidelity compared to the default state-preparation method in the Qiskit package. We furthermore demonstrate our method on IQM hardware with a square lattice connectivity, finding excellent fidelity, even with minimal noise mitigation. By significantly reducing gate depth for encoding, this work enables the experimental execution of applications on current and near-term hardware which would otherwise be reduced to noise before the first calculation step, shortening the time horizon to robust quantum utility.

item.title: Shaping Frequency-Bin Biphoton Correlations via Programmable Optical Frequency Combs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a model‑free, hardware‑in‑the‑loop optimizer can shape the joint spectral intensity of photon pairs generated by a programmable optical frequency comb, tuning up to 22 pump, signal and idler parameters with only two hardware evaluations per iteration. By achieving high Pearson correlations on 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5 frequency‑bin grids, it provides a practical route to reconfigurable, high‑dimensional frequency‑bin states that are essential for quantum communication, networking and sensing applications. The work builds on recent efforts to harness broadband nonlinear sources for scalable photonic qudits, but it currently controls only intensity—not spectral phase—so full two‑photon state engineering will still require phase‑sensitive characterization. Nonetheless, the demonstrated fast, parameter‑efficient shaping marks a significant step toward flexible quantum‑optical hardware that can be programmed on demand.

Programmable shaping of photon-pair spectral correlations is important for frequency-bin quantum information processing. However, achieving this control remains challenging in nonlinear optical systems without reliable forward models. Here, we demonstrate model-free, hardware-in-the-loop shaping of the measured joint spectral intensity of a cascaded photon-pair source driven by a programmable optical frequency comb. A blockwise simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation controller optimizes up to 22 pump, signal, and idler parameters. Each iteration requires only two accepted hardware evaluations, independent of the parameter count. The controller converges to diverse target patterns on 3$\times$3, 4$\times$4, and 5$\times$5 frequency-bin grids. The optimized distributions achieve Pearson correlations between 0.66 and 0.98 and classical overlap fidelities between 0.32 and 0.62. Cross-target similarity analysis confirms that the optimized patterns remain target-specific. Source characterization yields a maximum coincidence-to-accidental ratio of approximately 585. Accuracy is limited by pump-phase transfer, parasitic nonlinear background, waveshaper constraints, amplitude-only filtering, and measurement noise. Joint spectral intensity contains no spectral-phase information. Therefore, the results demonstrate control of measured frequency-bin populations and correlations, not complete reconstruction of the two-photon state. Phase-sensitive characterization is required to verify inter-bin coherence and quantify the entanglement dimensionality of the output state. Our results establish direct measurement feedback as a practical approach to reconfigurable frequency-bin correlation engineering when an accurate end-to-end model is unavailable.

item.title: Quantum subsets discrimination and key sifting with success probability one
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a long‑standing limitation of quantum cryptography by showing that error‑free discrimination between subsets of non‑orthogonal, even linearly dependent, states can be achieved with unit success probability—a feat previously thought impossible without sacrificing determinism. By turning the subset‑discrimination protocol into an alternative basis‑reconciliation step, it promises sifting efficiencies of 100 % for multi‑basis or high‑dimensional QKD schemes, potentially closing the gap between theoretical key rates and practical implementations. The result builds on recent advances in probabilistic orthogonalization and could reshape how future quantum‑secure networks handle state preparation and measurement, though experimental realization will hinge on implementing the required collective measurements with low overhead.

Non-distinguishability of non-orthogonal quantum states is the essential feature of quantum mechanics. In particular, one cannot deterministically orthogonalize the set of quantum states, while probabilistic orthogonalization is possible, including unambiguous state discrimination and discrimination between the subsets. Here, we propose a method for error-free subsets discrimination with significantly increased success probability, which may reach one even for non-orthogonal and linearly dependent input states. This method may be applied in quantum cryptography: An alternative basis reconciliation procedure is described, which may provide unit sifting probability even for a large number of bases and for non-orthogonal states within each basis.

item.title: Magic Can Superactivate Quantum Capacity
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that “magic”—the non‑stabilizer resource essential for universal quantum computation—can act as a catalyst that turns two otherwise useless channels into a conduit for genuine quantum information, extending the classic superactivation phenomenon to a new class of Clifford‑based convolutional channels. By linking magic to channel capacity through a concrete construction with mixed‑magic environments and half‑erasure auxiliaries, the work bridges abstract resource theories and practical communication models, suggesting that engineered noisy environments could be harnessed rather than merely mitigated. The result sharpens our understanding of what physical resources are truly required for quantum transmission and sets a benchmark for future protocols that aim to exploit non‑stabilizer noise as an asset rather than a liability.

Environmental magic can enable two channels with zero quantum capacity to transmit quantum information jointly. We establish this superactivation within a family of discrete quantum convolution channels with fixed Clifford interactions. For the couplings considered, stabilizer-mixture environments induce entanglement-breaking channels. We construct a mixed magic environment whose induced channel has positive private capacity and a Choi state with positive partial transpose, hence zero quantum capacity. A half-erasure auxiliary activates this channel through the Smith--Yard mechanism. Finite-block encoding and decoding over a self-complementary convolution auxiliary then realize a higher-dimensional erasure channel that still permits activation. We also bound the activated capacity by the modified relative entropy of magic of the main environment. Replacing either environment of the convolution pair by any stabilizer mixture makes the joint quantum capacity vanish, identifying environmental magic as a necessary resource on both sides for this realization.
